message:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.
response:
Good luck with it. A small rectangular floor is a sensible first tiling job, and you're clearly going in with a realistic view.

## What "lippage" means

Lippage is when one tile's edge sits higher than the tile next to it, so the surface has a tiny step instead of being perfectly flat. You can feel it with bare feet or catch it with a sock, and at a low angle the light picks it out as little shadows. On a floor, raised edges can also chip.

Long tiles like your 30 × 60 cm are more prone to it, because they often have a very slight bow along their length. That's why the tile shop may have mentioned it. Ways to avoid it are in the tips below.

## Grout colour for pale grey porcelain

Go for a **mid grey, one or two shades darker than the tile**. On a floor, white or very light grout darkens unevenly with foot traffic and looks grubby within weeks. A slightly darker grey hides that and still looks neat.

For the best stain resistance, consider a stain-resistant ("easy clean") grout, or an epoxy grout. Epoxy barely stains at all, but it's trickier to work with, so a good-quality stain-resistant cement grout is the friendlier choice for a first job.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Before.** The toilet should sit on the finished tiles. You won't have to cut tiles around the pan, the soil-pipe connection ends up at the right height, and if the toilet is ever replaced there's no untiled patch underneath.

## How many boxes

**Buy 4 boxes.**
- Floor area: 2.4 × 1.8 m = 4.32 m²
- Plus 10%: about 4.75 m²
- Each box: 8 tiles × 0.18 m² = 1.44 m²
- 4.75 ÷ 1.44 ≈ 3.3, so round up to 4

The numbers suggest exactly 3 boxes would cover the floor with no waste, since 24 tiles exactly fill 2.4 × 1.8 m. In practice they won't, for three reasons:
- **Grout gaps** push the last row past the wall, so it needs cutting.
- **Walls** are rarely perfectly square.
- **Extra cuts** are needed around the toilet pipe and the doorway.

The fourth box also leaves spares for breakages and future repairs. Keep a couple of tiles from the same batch, because colour can vary between batches.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi both, just a quick heads-up that we'll be cutting tiles for the bathroom floor on Saturday morning, so there'll be some noise from about 9 until lunchtime. Sorry, especially after you've put up with the skip on the drive for the past two weeks. Thanks so much for your patience, and do shout if the timing is a real problem.

Change the times to suit your plans.

## Three tips for a first floor

1. **Prepare the subfloor and dry-lay first.** The floor needs to be clean, solid and flat. If it's timber, it usually needs plywood or tile backer board over it. Lay the tiles out loose before mixing any adhesive. Start from the centre or a visible edge, and adjust so you don't end up with thin slivers at the doorway or along a wall.

2. **Get full adhesive coverage and avoid lippage.** Use the trowel size the adhesive packet recommends for 30 × 60 cm tiles. Also spread a thin layer on the back of each tile ("back-buttering"). Every so often, lift a freshly laid tile to check the adhesive is touching nearly the whole back. A cheap tile levelling clip system makes a big difference with long tiles. If you stagger the rows in a brick pattern, offset by no more than about a third of a tile (20 cm), not half. Because of that slight bow, half-offsets tend to cause lippage.

3. **Work in small sections and clean as you go.** Mix only as much adhesive as you can use in 20–30 minutes. Wipe adhesive off the tile faces and out of the joints before it sets, because cured adhesive is miserable to remove. Then stay off the floor for the curing time on the packet before grouting.

You'll probably find the cutting around the toilet pipe is the fiddliest part. Do those cuts while you're fresh, not at the end of the day, and practise on an offcut first.
